background.definition: Dementia with Lewy bodies is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia with associated core features of fluctuating cognition, hallucinations, and parkinsonism, resulting in slowly progressive and unrelenting dementia until death.

list.listitem: The incidence is 0.1% per year for the general population; 3.2% per year for all new dementia cases.
Lewy body dementia comprises approximately 4% of dementia cases diagnosed in the community.
The prevalence is less than 5% of general population.
Lewy bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions containing the protein synuclein) are found in the subcortical and cortical (frontotemporal) regions of the brain.
Mutations in glucocerebrosidase (GBA1) are a significant risk factor for DLB.
A total of 35% to 90% of patients with Lewy body dementia have concurrent Alzheimer-type pathology (especially plaques).
Deficits are present in both acetylcholine and dopamine production.
Patients typically present with dementia and core features of delirium,visual hallucinations, or parkinsonism. C
Inclusion of REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) improves the diagnostic accuracy.B
Usual evaluation for dementia is recommended. C
Use the Revised Criteria for the Clinical Diagnosis of Dementia with Lewy Bodies () and the Lewy Body Composite Risk Score to help with the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Dementia with Lewy bodies criteria, neuropsychiatric testing; SPECT or PET scan or MIBG myocardial scintigraphy can help to distinguish; visual hallucinations less prominent in AD
In dementia with Lewy bodies, dementia and Parkinson's disease must appear within 1 year of each other; tremor less prominent in DLB

list.listitem: See for guidelines for the diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies.
Patients typically present with Dementia, Delirium, and Visual hallucinations with parkinsonism (DDaVP mnemonic).
See for comparison of symptoms in dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease.

Patients may show more problems with the executive and visual-spatial aspects of the Mini-Mental State Examination; ie, may do worse with clock drawing than memory, which is the opposite of patients with Alzheimer’s disease. They may also have relative sparing of memory in early-stage disease.
Parkinsonism in DLB presents with bradykinesia, facial masking, rigidity, and postural instability. Tremor is uncommon.
Fluctuations in cognition may vary over minutes, hours, or days. Daytime sleepiness is prominent.
Visual hallucinations present early and are recurrent and well formed. These hallucinations are typically more concerning to the caregiver than to the patient.
Visual hallucinations together with memory impairment may be the best clinical predictor of DLB and its differetiation from Alzheimer's.
Routine dementia evaluation is recommended, including B12 level, thyroid-stimulating hormone, screening for depression, and screening for syphilis.
Consider tests for metabolic causes of delirium such as comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC, and drug levels.
Obtain neuroimaging (MR) to rule out surgically treatable causes of dementia and to help differentiate from Alzheimer's disease.
Low uptake MIBG scintigraphy may be the most sensitive test. Others include [(123)I]FP-CIT SPECT, occipital hypometabolism on FDG-PET and preservation of medial temporal lobe structures on MRI.
Consider neuropsychological testing, which may be helpful in differentiating dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer’s disease from normal aging.
Applying the Lewy Body Composite Risk Score may increase the likelihood of determining whether Lewy Bodies are contributing pathology to the dementia.
See algorithm in for a recommended approach to the patient with suspected dementia with Lewy bodies.
Cholinesterase inhibitors may be helpful and are the usual first-line therapy. A
Avoid typical neuroleptic agents and anticholinergics, and be cautious with newer antipsychotics. B
Develop a problem list with the patient and/or caregiver to prioritize treatments, as improvement in one area may come at the expense of another. C
Cholinesterase inhibitors may be helpful.

In a large prospective cohort study study, over 3 years of follow-up, men who took terazosin, doxazosin, or alfuzosin were less likely to develop Lewy body dementia than those who took tamsulosin or 5ARIs. After 3 years, rates of diagnosis per 10,000 person-years were 5.3 for terazosin, doxazosin, or alfuzosin compared with 8.9 in those taking tamsulosin.
Avoid anticholinergic agents (diphenhydramine, meclizine, oxybutynin, highly anticholinergic tricyclics) and typical neuroleptics.

A systematic review of 53 studies with over 25,000 participants concluded that adults with neurocognitive disorders who take cholinesterase inhibitors are less likely to have falls but more likely to experience syncope than adults who take placebo.
Be cautious regarding the use (if at all) of atypical antipsychotics.
Memantine may be helpful.
Use low-dose levodopa for parkinsonism only if needed to manage movement disorder.
Postural hypotension may respond to midodrine and fludrocortisone.
Consider clonazepam or memantine for REM sleep behavior disorder.
Yi-Gan San, a traditional Chinese herbal medicine, was found to be helpful for cholinesterase inhibitor-resistant visual hallucinations in one small study.
Therapy may be helpful to improve sensory impairments, to provide structure and routine, and to teach behavioral interventions.
Data from clinical trials are lacking, though.

An Italian guideline (2025) recommends aerobic and nonaerobic exercise for persons with mild cognitive impairment and with mild and moderate dementia. The panel supports the use of music and art therapy.

The guideline provides a long list of popular “treatments” and interventions that are ineffective, including ketogenic diets; aromatherapy; various “formulas,” often containing omega-3 fatty acids, various vitamins, selenium, and so forth; ginseng, gingko biloba, and other herbal supplements; light therapy; acupuncture; laser therapy; and therapeutic robots.
The natural history of dementia with Lewy bodies is of relatively rapid progression over 1 to 5 years. B
Frequent follow up (ie, every 3 months) is recommended to manage disease complications and adjust medications. C

feature.caption: Revised Criteria for the Clinical Diagnosis of Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB).
feature.feature_body:
1 Central feature (essential for a diagnosis of possible or probable DLB) Dementia defined as progressive cognitive decline of sufficient magnitude to interfere with normal social or occupational function. Prominent or persistent memory impairment may not necessarily occur in the early stages but is usually evident with progression. Deficits on tests of attention, executive function, and visuospatial ability may be especially prominent.
2 Core features (two core features are sufficient for a diagnosis of probable DLB, one for possible DLB) Fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness -Recurrent visual hallucinations that are typically well formed and detailed -Spontaneous features of parkinsonism.
3 Suggestive features (If one or more of these is present in the presence of one or more core features, a diagnosis of probable DLB can be made. In the absence of any core features, one or more suggestive features is sufficient for possible DLB. Probable DLB should not be diagnosed on the basis of suggestive features alone.) -REM sleep behavior disorder -Severe neuroleptic sensitivity -Low dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia demonstrated by SPECT or PET imaging.
4 Supportive features (commonly present but not proven to have diagnostic specificity) Repeated falls and syncope -Transient, unexplained loss of consciousness -Severe autonomic dysfunction, e.g., orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence -Hallucinations in other modalities -Systematized delusions -Depression -Relative preservation of medial temporal lobe structures on CT/MRI scan -Generalized low uptake on SPECT/PET perfusion scan with reduced occipital activity -Abnormal (low uptake) MIBG myocardial scintigraphy -Prominent slow wave activity on EEG with temporal lobe transient sharp waves.
5 A diagnosis of DLB is less likely In the presence of cerebrovascular disease evident as focal neurologic signs or on brain imagingIn the presence of any other physical illness or brain disorder sufficient to account in part or in total for the clinical pictureIf parkinsonism only appears for the first time at a stage of sever dementia.
6 Temporal sequence of symptoms DLB should be diagnosed when dementia occurs before or concurrently with parkinsonism (if it is present). The term Parkinson disease dementia (PDD) should be used to describe dementia that occures in the cotext of well-established parkinson disease. In a practice setting, the term that is most appropriate to the clinical situation should be used and generic terms such as LB disease are often helpful. In research studies in which distinction needs to be made between DLB and PDD, the existing 1-year rule between the onset of dementia and parkinsonism DLB continues to be recommended. Adoption of other time periods will simply confound data pooling or comparison between studies. In other research settings that may include clinicopathologic studies and clinical trials, both clinical phenotypes may be considered collectively under categories such as LB diseaser or alpha-synucleinopathy.
From: McKeith IG, Dickson DW, Lowe J, et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: third report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology 2005;65:1863–1872.

feature.caption: Comparison of Dementia with Lewy Bodies with Alzheimer’s Disease and Parkinson’s Disease.
feature.feature_body:
Signs of Disease Alzheimer’s Disease Dementia with Lewy Bodies Parkinson’s Disease
Clinical Signs
Dementia Early impairment of memory and attention Early disturbance in attention and visual perception No early impairment
Delirium Occasional Typical Rare
Visual hallucinations Occasional Typical Occasional
Delusions Typical Typical Occasional
Parkinsonism Rare Within 1 year of onset of dementia First manifestation
Autonomic dysfunction Rare Typical Typical
Rigor Occasional Typical Typical
Bradykinesia Occasional Typical Typical
Tremor Rare Occasional Typical
Pathologic Signs
Neuritic plaques Typical Typical Rare
Neurofibrillary tangles Typical Occasional Rare
Cortical Lewy bodies Rare Typical Occasional
Subcortical Lewy bodies Rare Typical Typical
Biochemical Signs
Cholinergic deficit Typical Typical Occasional
Dopaminergic deficit Rare Typical Typical
From Neef D, Walling AD. Dementia with Lewy bodies: an emerging disease. Am Fam Physician 2006;73:1223–1229.
